classification.difficultyReason: Combine quarter-circle and triangular areas, recognising cancellation and subtracting regions below the axis.

content.prompt: Use area formulae to find $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx$, given the following sketches of $f(x)$.

spec.description: Two unit quarter-circle arcs joined by straight segments, with half-unit unnumbered ticks and dashed coordinate guides.
spec.mathematics: Unit circle centred at (0,0) from (0,1) to (1,0); segments to (2,-1) and (3,1); unit circle centred at (3,0) from (3,1) to (4,0).
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied graph only; no areas or answers shown.

answer.worked:
The equal triangles above and below the axis between $x=2$ and $x=3$ cancel. Each curved region is a quarter-circle of radius $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx&=\frac{\pi(1)^2}{4}-\frac12(1)(1)+0+\frac{\pi(1)^2}{4}\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12.\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Concave-up unit quarter-circle arc, descending straight segment and lower unit quarter-circle arc, with half-unit ticks and dashed guides.
spec.mathematics: Circle centred at (0,1) from (0,0) to (1,1); line through (2,0) to (3,-1); circle centred at (3,0) from (3,-1) to (4,0).
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied graph only; no areas or answers shown.

answer.worked:
From $x=0$ to $x=1$, the area is a unit square minus a unit quarter-circle. The equal triangles from $x=1$ to $x=3$ cancel. The final quarter-circle lies below the axis.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx&=\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+\frac12-\frac12-\frac{\pi}{4}\\&=1-\frac{\pi}{2}.\end{aligned}$$
